To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
alcohol-dependent patients who are aggressive, impulsive and show antisocial behaviors have a stronger intensity dependence of auditory evoked responses than patients who do not have these behaviors.

patients with antisocial personality disorder (ASPD) and alcoholism show stronger intensity dependence of cortical auditory-evoked responses than patients with ASPD and no alcoholism, and patients with ASPD show stronger intensity dependence than patients without ASPD and alcoholism.
patients with antisocial personality traits have a stronger intensity dependence of the auditory-evoked responses than patients without these personality traits.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the brain serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT) system is involved in the pathogenesis of antisocial tendencies and alcoholism.
the neurobiological basis of alcohol-related disorders, with special regard to the role of serotonergic neurotransmitters.
the question, which biological factors are involved in the pathophysiology of alcoholism and which of these factors are related to the development of antisocial tendencies and impulsive behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the intensity dependence of primary auditory cortex responses is a marker for serotonergic neurotransmitter dysfunction in alcoholism, but not in other psychiatric disorders.

alcohol-dependent patients who show a strong intensity dependence of auditory cortical responses and antisocial behavior form a subgroup, which is supposed to be characterized by a dysfunction of central serotoninergic neurotransmission.

the intensity dependence of auditory-evoked responses is not related to alcoholism per se but is related to a subgroup of alcoholics, which is characterized by antisocial behavior and low serotonergic function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the N1/P2 component of the auditory-evoked potentials in alcohol-dependent patients is modulated by a strong intensity dependence of the responses of the primary auditory cortex.
the strong intensity dependence is a marker for the serotonergic dysfunction and the antisocial tendencies are a consequence of the serotonergic dysregulation.
the N1/P2 response to auditory stimuli is an indicator of serotonergic neurotransmition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain serotonin system may play a role in antisocial behavior.

we have found that alcoholics with antisocial personality disorder and a strong intensity dependence of auditory-evoked responses of primary cortices are characterized by a dysfunction of the central serotonergic system.

alcohol-dependent patients who have a strong intensity dependence of their cortical auditory responses and antisocial tendencies may form a subgroup with serotonergic hypodopaminergic neurotransmission.
